parts.name: On the waterfront
parts.stand: At the water's edge in Little Venice, looking along the row of houses.

paras.t: This is Little Venice, also called Alefkandra, at the far western edge of town. Look at the houses: rows of them right on the waterfront, with their balconies hanging over the sea.
Mind your step along the edge. When the wind is up, waves can splash over, and wet stone gets slippery.
They're two and three stories high and stand like a wall above the sea. Pick out the colorful wooden balconies.
How old are they? The first went up in the mid-18th century, though you'll see them loosely called medieval.

parts.name: Captains and pirates
parts.stand: Stay where you can see the foot of the houses, where the walls meet the water.

paras.t: These houses first belonged to rich merchants and sea captains. Down at the bottom, little doors opened straight onto the sea and into storage below.
And that started a story. With doors like that, the story goes, people believed the owners were secretly pirates. It's a rumor, not a record, but you can see how it began.
It wasn't a wild idea for its time. Up to the end of the 18th century, Mykonos was a thriving trading town, and pirates raided it again and again.

parts.name: Sunset row
parts.stand: Turn and look back up the hill toward the windmills.

paras.t: Up on the hill above the harbor stand the windmills. Today some of these old houses are bars, cafes, little shops and galleries.
This is said to be one of the most romantic spots on the island. In the evening, people gather here to watch the sunset, and artists come to paint this coastline.

The waterfront wasn't always this lively. The island's economy faded in the late 19th century, especially after the Corinth Canal opened, and many Mykonians left to find work, many of them in the United States. Then the visitors came. In the 1960s, the international jet set discovered Mykonos, and by the 2000s it was one of the most expensive islands in Greece.
Picture a captain's family at one of these windows, watching the sea for a sail coming home. People still stand here looking out at the same water. Only now, most of us are waiting for the sun.
